objectives: Compare Unity / Unreal / Godot / custom engines.
Reason about build + deployment for multiple platforms.

slides.title: Major game engines + their niches
slides.body:
**Unreal Engine** (Epic Games, free below \$1M):
- Industry workhorse for AAA + cinematics. C++ + Blueprint visual scripting.
- Strengths: graphics (Lumen real-time GI, Nanite virtualized geometry), MetaHuman face tech, MetaSounds audio.
- Used by: Fortnite, Cyberpunk 2077 (now), Black Myth Wukong, many AAA.
- 5% royalty above \$1M revenue.

**Unity** (Unity Technologies):
- C# scripting; ECS (DOTS) + traditional MonoBehaviour.
- Strengths: mobile + AR/VR; large indie community; large asset store.
- Used by: ~50% of mobile games, Pokemon GO, Among Us, Beat Saber, Genshin Impact (Unity build).
- Free up to \$200K revenue + then paid tiers.

**Godot** (open-source, MIT):
- GDScript (Python-like), C#, or C++. Lightweight.
- Strengths: open-source, no royalty, small download, integrated editor.
- Used by: indie games (Brotato, Cassette Beasts). 2024 explosion in adoption after Unity pricing controversies.

**CryEngine, Lumberyard** (Amazon's CryEngine fork): less popular than past.

**Custom engines** (in-house):
- **id Tech** (id Software): Doom Eternal, Doom 2016, Rage.
- **REDengine** (CD Projekt): Witcher 3, Cyberpunk 2077 (now moving to Unreal).
- **Decima** (Guerrilla Games): Horizon Zero Dawn, Death Stranding.
- **Anvil** (Ubisoft): Assassin's Creed series.
- **Frostbite** (EA / DICE): Battlefield, Star Wars Battlefront, FIFA, Madden.
- **RAGE** (Rockstar): GTA V, Red Dead Redemption 2.

**Custom engines** advantages: tuned for the studio's games, IP-controllable, performance-optimized. Disadvantages: maintenance cost, dev-onboarding burden, third-party-tool integration challenges.

**Trend**: more studios move to Unreal for shared tech (CD Projekt's switch in 2022). Custom engines for the largest studios with long-term franchises (Rockstar, Ubisoft) still preferred.

slides.title: Asset pipeline
slides.body:
Games have huge asset budgets — models, textures, audio, animations, levels. The **asset pipeline** processes them from artist DCC (Digital Content Creation tool) to optimized runtime format.

**Typical pipeline**:
1. **Source**: artist creates in DCC (Maya, Blender, ZBrush for models; Photoshop, Substance for textures; FMOD / Wwise for audio).
2. **Export**: source format (FBX, OBJ, PNG, WAV) saved to source-control (Git LFS, Perforce, SVN).
3. **Cooking / building**: engine converts to platform-specific optimized format (compressed textures, mesh LOD, baked lighting). Hours-to-days for AAA build.
4. **Packaging**: bundle into IPA / APK / pak files for platform distribution.
5. **Distribution**: Steam, PlayStation Store, Xbox Live, App Store, Google Play.

**Texture compression**:
- **BC1/BC3 (S3TC / DXTn)**: PC desktop. Lossy block compression, 4-8 bits/pixel.
- **ASTC**: mobile + modern desktop. Adaptive block size. Better quality/size.
- **ETC2**: Android default. Decent quality.
- **PVRTC**: legacy iOS.
- Each platform has its preferred format; assets often built into multiple variants.

**Mesh formats**: vertex buffers + index buffers. Vertex attributes (position, normal, UV, tangent, bone weights). LOD levels for distance-based detail reduction.

**Audio**: streamed (music, dialogue) vs cached (SFX). Compressed (OGG Vorbis, Opus). Spatial audio for VR.

**Build sizes**: AAA console games are 30-150 GB. Includes uncompressed dialogue for cinematic quality, 4K textures, multiplatform variants. Mobile games typically 100 MB - 5 GB.

**Streaming**: load assets ON DEMAND as the player moves through the world. Open-world games (GTA V, Cyberpunk) stream entire worlds. Async loading + memory management is engineering-heavy.

slides.title: Build + deployment + live ops
slides.body:
**Multi-platform builds**: PC (Win/Linux/Mac), PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/Series X|S, Switch, iOS, Android, Steam Deck. Each has different APIs (DX12, Metal, Vulkan, PS5 GNM, Xbox D3D12).

**CI/CD for games**:
- **Trunk-based development**: monorepo with feature branches.
- **Build farm**: per-platform builders (often Windows/Mac VMs for Apple, dedicated PS / Xbox dev kits).
- **Nightly + per-commit builds**: tested by QA + automated tests.
- **Build size**: AAA console build can take 4-8 hours; PC 1-2 hours.
- **Cooking**: convert assets to platform-specific format (Unreal: 'cook for X'). Hours-long process.

**Distribution platforms**:
- **Steam**: PC dominant. SteamWorks SDK. ~30% revenue share (or 25% above \$10M, 20% above \$50M).
- **Epic Games Store**: lower 12% cut.
- **PlayStation / Xbox / Switch**: console certification ('cert'). Strict requirements (no crashes, performance targets, language localization). Days-to-weeks of cert testing.
- **App Store / Google Play**: mobile. 30% (or 15% after first year).

**Live ops**: post-launch operations.
- **Patches**: bug fixes, balance changes, new features.
- **Content updates**: seasonal events, new characters, maps.
- **Anti-cheat**: BattlEye, EAC, Vanguard. Kernel-level (controversial) or user-space (Riot Vanguard, Valorant).
- **Telemetry + analytics**: in-game events recorded for balance + bug analysis. Privacy compliance (GDPR, CCPA).
- **Community management**: Discord, Reddit, forums. Communication channels.
- **Crash reporting + telemetry**: backtrace.io, Sentry, custom systems.

**Live-service economics**: games as services (Fortnite, Apex, Valorant) earn through cosmetics + battle passes. \$100M+ monthly revenue achievable. Requires sustained engineering investment after launch.

**Modding + community content**: Skyrim's Creation Engine, GTA V's third-party modding (RP servers), Minecraft. Mod ecosystems extend game life by years.

question.question: Choose an engine for a project
question.goal: Project: 3D third-person action-adventure for PC + console + mobile. Team: 30 developers, including 20 with C++ experience + 10 with C#.

steps.prompt: Engine candidates: Unreal (C++), Unity (C#), Godot (GDScript/C#/C++). Team strengths align with which?

options: Unreal: leans on C++ majority, multi-platform mature, AAA-quality graphics. Unity could work for the C# side but less mature for AAA on console.

steps.reveal: Unreal: strong fit for C++ team + multi-platform AAA. C# team could work in Blueprint (visual scripting) or learn C++.

steps.prompt: Mobile target is also required. Unreal's mobile support is good but heavier than Unity. Implications?

options: Either: (1) Accept Unreal's mobile compromises (larger app size, more constrained graphics); or (2) Build mobile version in Unity, share game logic via libraries — operationally complex but possible.

steps.reveal: Unreal mobile is viable but app sizes typically 200MB+ vs Unity's possible 50-100MB. For AAA-style mobile (Genshin-quality), Unreal's overhead may be acceptable. For lighter mobile, Unity's better fit. Major decision; affects build pipeline + monetization.

steps.prompt: Royalty: Unreal 5% above \$1M; Unity tiered. For a \$50M-revenue game, royalty cost?

options: Unreal: ~\$2.5M (5% of \$49M above threshold). Unity Personal: free below \$200K, then licensed seats + Pro fees. Pricing comparable at high revenue but Unity has had pricing controversies (Sept 2023 'install fee' debacle).

steps.reveal: Royalty math + business considerations factor in. Unreal's 5% royalty is well-known. Unity's recent (now-reversed) pricing changes drove some studios to evaluate alternatives. Godot has zero royalty (MIT).

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Engine choice = team skills + targets + economics + roadmap}}$$ Each engine has its niche. Unreal for AAA + photorealistic. Unity for mobile + AR/VR + many indies. Godot for open-source + small projects. Custom for large studios with long-term franchises. The decision affects 5+ years of dev cost + risk; switching mid-project (CD Projekt's 2022 announcement) is rare + expensive.

question.question: Why are 'live-service' games (Fortnite, Apex, Valorant) so dominant economically despite being 'free'?
options: Free + cosmetic monetization: huge player base (no purchase barrier); cosmetic items + battle passes monetize 5-10% of users at ~\$50-200/year/user; constant content updates retain users; network effects (friends play) drive retention. \$1B+ annual revenue possible.
question.explanation: Live-service model: cheap (or free) entry + ongoing monetization via cosmetics, battle passes, character unlocks. Fortnite: \$5B+ revenue in 2018. Apex: \$1B+ annually. Valorant: similar. Combines retention engineering (events, seasons, social features) + cosmetic monetization that doesn't pay-to-win. Requires sustained engineering investment (post-launch dev team often larger than launch team). Many studios pivoted from pure-product games to live services (Destiny, Diablo, MMO).

slides.workedSolution: Free + cosmetic monetization removes purchase barrier → massive player base. ~5-10% of players spend, average \$50-200/year. Network effects: 'my friends play' is the strongest retention factor. Constant content = retention + monetization opportunity. Engineering investment: post-launch dev team often equals or exceeds launch team. Risks: live-ops fatigue, content treadmills, monetization controversies. But the economics dominate when it works.

question.question: AAA build with 100 GB assets, asset processing at 1 GB/sec. Build time?
When to build a custom engine
question.prompt: A new studio is starting an action-adventure series intended to span 10+ years + multiple titles. Walk through whether to use Unreal or build a custom engine.
Explain in two or three sentences why most studios use a third-party engine (Unreal, Unity) rather than building custom.
question.rubric: Mentions that custom engines require dedicated graphics + tools + platform engineering teams (cost millions/year); Unreal + Unity provide world-class graphics + extensive tooling for free (or royalty); time-to-market + risk reduction are massive; only the largest studios with long-running franchises (Rockstar, EA, Ubisoft) justify custom. The pattern has accelerated since Unreal 5's release.
